title: Dord, the word that never was
hook: A word that sat in a major dictionary for years and meant nothing at all.
peek: In 1934 Webster's New International Dictionary listed "dord", meaning density. The word did not exist. It came from a misread note card, and it stayed in print for years before an editor noticed it had no history.
lede: The second edition of Webster's New International Dictionary, published in 1934, included the entry "dord", a term in physics and chemistry for density. Nobody had ever used it. The word had been created inside the dictionary office by a filing slip, and it took several years for anyone to notice.

bullets.text: A 1931 note card meant to say that "D or d" could be an abbreviation for density. The card was filed with the words instead of the abbreviations, and the spaces were lost, so "D or d" became "dord".
In 1939 an editor noticed that dord had no word history listed. Checking back revealed the mistake, and the entry was dropped from later printings, though copies with it still turn up.

Dictionary makers call entries born from errors "ghost words", a phrase the scholar Walter Skeat used in the 1880s. Dord is the best-known example, and the Merriam-Webster editor Philip Babcock Gove later wrote up its full history.
